newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein leaders win seats in British parliament.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein leaders win seats in British parliament.

text.p: Gerry Adams and Martin McGuinness, leaders of the hardline Irish nationalist party Sinn Fein, scored landmark victories in the British general election, winning seats for Northern Ireland districts at Westminster.

Results declared on Friday showed Adams, head of the political wing of the outlawed Irish Republican Army (IRA), won a seat in Belfast and McGuinness, one of Sinn Fein's senior strategists, was elected in the rural Mid-Ulster seat.
It is the first time in more than 40 years that Sinn Fein have achieved two victories in Northern Ireland seats for the British parliament.

Adams dislodged the sitting moderate nationalist, Joe Hendron, of the Social Democratic and Labour Party, giving Sinn Fein its first national election seat for five years. In 1992 Adams lost the seat to Hendron.
McGuinness unseated William McCrea, a member of the hardline pro-British Democratic Unionist Party.
Sinn Fein is the legal political arm of the IRA, which has waged a guerrilla war for 28 years to try to end British rule in Northern Ireland.
Both Sinn Fein candidates are pledged not to take up their seats in the London legislature because they refuse to recognise Britain's right to rule in the province.

Their wins were highlights of a poll for the province's 18 parliamentary seats which otherwise seemed to be dividing along traditional lines, with majority Protestants voting for "Unionist" parties and minority Catholics backing Irish nationalists.

Adams said his election was a message from his nationalist stronghold of West Belfast that Sinn Fein should be treated the same as other political groups and allowed into all-party talks on bringing a lasting peace to the province.

"This election sends a very clear message to those in high places in London and in Dublin and everywhere else that the people of West Belfast have a right to be treated as equals, have a right to a future as equals," he said.
"This election makes it a compulsion for all of those in the establishment in London and in Dublin urgently to restore a proper peace process on the basis of equality," Adams said.
Britain and Ireland insist Sinn Fein will not be given a seat in talks until the IRA ends hostilities, which it resumed in February 1996 after a 17-month truce.

Mo Mowlam, the woman tipped to be Britain's next Northern Ireland Secretary, made it clear shortly after the Labour Party coasted to a landslide win in the national poll that she would adhere to that line.

"We have made it very clear that none of my colleagues will have any contact with Sinn Fein while the IRA makes that impossible. However there is a door open there and they know the conditions through which they will facilitate others to pass through it," she said in a BBC radio interview.

In Dublin, Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said Britain's incoming Labour government and new Prime Minister Tony Blair could, along with Dublin, bring fresh drive to the search for a Northern Ireland peace.

Bruton told reporters: "I think the fact that we now in Britain have a government with a strong majority will enable it to tackle issues with resolution in regard to Northern Ireland...to inject new urgency into the talks process."
Bruton agrees with Britain that an IRA truce must precede Sinn Fein's admission to the existing multi-party talks that adjourned in deadlock in March.
